sections.title: What is ViewPoint
sections.lede: ViewPoint (the hackathon build of MetaViewer) is a desktop where AI agents open and drive real programs, each inside its own capsule, while a person keeps the keyboard. Between what an agent proposes and what reaches the screen sits an admission core, so every action ends in a verified receipt or in a typed refusal, failure or uncertain outcome, never in a silent success.

blocks.title: Capsules and the wall
blocks.body: A capsule is a named live surface paired with an operator-created identity and browser profile. Using the OpenSuperficies substrate, each browser capsule runs Xvfb, a window manager, streaming, and a browser inside one capsule bounded by loopback ports. The operator opens capsules on a wall—such as a 2x2 grid of 4 named capsules—while the configured ceiling is 16 capsules. The wall displays frames and state, but holds no admission authority, and Host program capsules are explicitly not isolated.

blocks.title: Admission instead of blind input
blocks.body: Conventional desktop automation fires clicks at whichever window holds focus and assumes success. ViewPoint enforces a five-step loop: see, propose, admit, act, and verify. An agent observes a fresh frame, proposes an input bound to that frame's digest and generation, and waits for the core to check ownership, lease, and budget before dispatching to the native adapter. Failures return typed errors—INPUT_UNCERTAIN, STALE_FRAME, or VERIFICATION_FAILED—and stop the sequence so an uncertain action is never silently counted as success.

blocks.title: The operator keeps the keyboard
blocks.body: Agents execute hidden on a private display while the operator keeps the desktop keyboard and watches through a viewer. Because no component in the stack reads profiles, cookies, or credentials, the operator signs in manually inside a capsule before handing control to an agent; logins persist in the capsule store across restarts. Security boundaries stay explicit: vp_navigate accepts only https:// URLs and refuses non-empty queries or fragments, because the capsule's URL readback omits them by privacy design. It rejects literal private, loopback and link-local hosts before any input; DNS names are left to the capsule egress policy. CAPTCHAs are not bypassed.

blocks.title: Handing over: human ↔ agent
blocks.body: The operator can reclaim control per capsule or in bulk. In measured runs, bulk Pass all to Humans brought 4/4 views ready in 51 s, allowing live typing to reach the page, and Pass all to Agents returned capsules to agent control. After fixing a round-trip input bug, a handover test verified 4/4 agent navigations plus 1 task after return. However, the default workflow still restarts before each take in about 3 min for clean state, and seamless return is not claimed as the default.

blocks.title: MCP for any AI client
blocks.body: External AI clients connect through a stdio MCP bridge rather than calling native executors directly. The MCP layer exposes identity management tools—list, create, set_label, and delete with confirmation—alongside bounded browser operations including vp_navigate, vp_browser_task, and vp_read_page. Because the MCP server only delegates observation and proposal calls to the core and never owns admission, all proposals remain subject to live frame checks and core verification. Measured single-capsule reliability reached 156/158 verified navigations, while query or fragment URLs were refused in 30-54 ms.

sections.title: One core admits every action
sections.lede: ViewPoint places a Rust admission core between AI agents and the program capsules they drive. Agents observe a frame identified by its digest, propose an action bound to that observation, and wait for a verified receipt or a typed failure. Capture, pixel description and planning sit outside admission, and the operator keeps the keyboard.

blocks.title: Who does what
blocks.body: The operator opens capsules, signs in manually, and watches or reclaims control through the viewer while agents work on a private display. Agents connect over stdio to the viewpoint-agent MCP server, which exposes vp_list_capsules, vp_navigate, vp_browser_task, vp_read_page, and capsule identity tools for list, create, set_label, and confirm-gated delete. The MCP server delegates via mvctl and bounded mw_run to the Rust core, which owns admission and verification. A Go native adapter manages OpenSuperficies browser capsules and publishes frames, while the private vision engine describes pixels and the wender-agent planner proposes plans without admission authority.

blocks.title: The action loop
blocks.body: Every browser action follows a closed five-step loop: see, propose, admit, act, and verify. First, the agent observes the named surface and receives a fresh frame carrying a sha256 digest and generation counter. Next, it submits a proposal bound to that frame digest and generation. The core checks ownership, frame freshness, lease state, policy, and budget before admitting dispatch to the native adapter. After execution, the core recomputes verification from capture evidence and returns a verified receipt or stops with a typed failure. Navigation via vp_navigate executes three bound proposals in sequence, or two from a genuine blank page.

blocks.title: The vision engine and what it may not do
blocks.body: The vision engine is a deterministic, integer-only visual QA component. Its pipeline goes from a frame manifest to a tile grid, descriptors, change classes, regions, a temporal group of frames, a token-bounded judge pack and a visual memory, and it answers in closed JSON. Agents reach it through the vision skill: look returns the frame with numbered marks, act sends a key or click and checks that something changed (exit code 3 when nothing did), and every call leaves a receipt. It describes pixels and never admits an action, because a frame digest proves which bytes were seen, not what they mean.

blocks.title: Typed verdicts, never silent success
blocks.body: ViewPoint fails closed with typed verdicts rather than counting uncertain actions as successes. During execution, STALE_FRAME, INPUT_UNCERTAIN, and VERIFICATION_FAILED halt the sequence so an agent never blindly replays input. URLs with non-empty queries or fragments are refused in 30 to 54 milliseconds with zero browser input as URL_QUERY_UNOBSERVABLE or URL_FRAGMENT_UNOBSERVABLE, and browser readback mismatches raise MW_BROWSER_TEXT_MISMATCH. Capsule management enforces CAPSULE_LIMIT_REACHED at 16 capsules, NO_FREE_PROFILE, NO_IDENTITY, IDENTITY_LIST_UNAVAILABLE, and refusals for unknown identities, active capsule deletion, or wrong delete confirmation, while held window tools return TAKE_NOT_RUNNING.

blocks.title: Trust boundaries and takeover
blocks.body: Only the core admits actions and verifies receipts; the UI wall, MCP bridge, vision engine, and planner hold no admission authority. Operators sign in manually so software never reads profiles, cookies, or credentials, and no CAPTCHA bypass exists. Navigation accepts only https URLs and rejects literal private, loopback, and link-local hosts before input, relying on capsule egress policy for DNS names. The AX surface strips queries and fragments by privacy design, bounding verification to document scheme, host, port, and path. Bulk switching hands four capsules to human views in 51 seconds, while the Cloud Run replay gateway remains target-only without browser actuation.

blocks.title: The journal and two capacity cliffs
blocks.body: The core appends state transitions and frame witnesses to a journal whose transition sequence, previous-record digests and required witnesses are checked before updating authority state, while transport anti-replay blocks duplicate or non-increasing sender sequences and mv-replay checks archive closure offline. Testing exposed two deterministic cliffs, both failing closed. First, a 128-entry proposal-witness table evicted the newest unsettled entry starting at proposal 129; evicting settled entries first raised single-capsule reliability to 156 of 158 verified navigations. Second, raising the session journal budget eliminated round-5 session termination, moving the four-capsule five-round flow from 11 of 15 to 12 of 15 verified searches.

blocks.title: Rewind: two kinds
blocks.body: In the multi-agent Blender takes, a reference rewind (Claude's units R0 to R4, declared) checkpoints the shared scene and restores it when the judge rejects an edit; every rewind in those takes matched its checkpoint digest and the audit found 0 violations. Separately, ViewPoint's ARM64 MicroVM developer implementation defines Pause, Resume, Mark, Back and Stop over a protected RAM checkpoint ring capped at 1 GiB. Restoring reverts guest memory and machine state, but cannot undo completed network requests, host files or the journal. It needs protected local artifacts and an admitted ARM64/KVM backend; live demonstrations are maintainer-reported and not claimed here.

sections.title: Think in parallel, act in turns
sections.lede: Agents look at their frames and plan in parallel, then their actions go through one admitted lane, one at a time. On the browser wall, the four capsules share ViewPoint's core-admitted input lane. In the Blender takes, which run on a private display outside the ViewPoint program lane, a Claude-written broker, auction, judge and checkpointed rewind do the same job while Gemini agents write the scripts and intents.

blocks.title: Why one lane
blocks.body: Strict lockstep execution stalls on the slowest peer, and live GUIs or Blender viewports lack cheap deterministic rollback. ViewPoint's queue model separates concurrent observation from exclusive actuation so parallelism comes from multiple agents planning against read-only frames rather than splitting the single executor. In four-capsule browser runs, Gemini agents read their own isolated capsules in parallel and queue actions onto one shared admitted input lane. When another agent holds the lane, a waiting caller receives AGENT_BUSY with nothing sent, waits its turn, and re-observes current state before proposing.

blocks.title: Turn queue specification and lifecycle phases
blocks.body: The turn-queue specification defines a discrete-event loop with five phases per integer action_seq tick: CAPTURE publishes an immutable frame, INTENT lets agents enqueue commands citing based_on_frame, ADMIT validates only the queue head against broker state, EXECUTE grants one exclusive GUI or script window, and CLOSE records a typed verdict and frame N+1. Design targets specify an 8-event bounded FIFO per agent, round-robin turn order, and hold limits of 15 s to confirm, 60 s for a GUI turn, and 120 s per script job, though these timeout ceilings are uncalibrated targets.

blocks.title: Shared lane verdicts in wall take 2049
blocks.body: In the 2049_wall_multigemini take, four Gemini 4 Hydrogen (High) agents browsed four isolated capsules across 180 logged events. All four agents logged AGENT_BUSY waits (including C-github, D-gemini, A-arxiv, and B-wikipedia yielding to the active turn), while navigations took 30 to 99 s under four-agent contention. Auditing only tool verdicts rather than agent self-reports—because Agent A's final answer said 'verified 6 of 6'—shows verified lane actions of A-arxiv 3 of 5, B-wikipedia 4 of 5, C-github 2 of 4, and D-gemini 2 of 3.

blocks.title: Typed refusals across multi-agent wall runs
blocks.body: ViewPoint core admission reports typed failures instead of silent success whenever an action cannot be verified. In 2049_wall_multigemini, D-gemini triggered URL_FRAGMENT_UNOBSERVABLE with zero input sent because the capsule accessibility surface strips fragments by privacy design; B-wikipedia logged MW_PROGRAM_NO_VISIBLE_EFFECT, and A-arxiv hit MW_STALE_FRAME_EXHAUSTED as well as INPUT_UNCERTAIN on its last navigation. Across the 2035_wall_multigemini and 2021_wall_multigemini takes, the shared lane similarly surfaced STALE_FRAME, URL_FRAGMENT_UNOBSERVABLE, and INPUT_UNCERTAIN as explicit typed refusals and failures.

blocks.title: Auction scheduling, judging, and verified rewinds
blocks.body: In multi-agent Blender builds, a Claude-declared infrastructure stack runs a Vickrey aging auction (vickrey_aging_v1), a verification judge, and checkpointed rewinds while four Gemini 4 Hydrogen (High) agents author bpy scripts and camera key intents. During 1552_platform37, 1590 log records captured 329 auction, 77 auction_settle, 62 judge, 47 ckpt, and 126 txn events. Out of 67 agent events, 41 closed STATE_VERIFIED and 5 VERIFIED, while 16 hit ALL_REJECTED and 5 hit STALE_FRAME. All 17 rewinds passed with digest_match true (0 violations), including reverting a director-injected wrong edit flagged EXPECT_MISMATCH and DELTA_OUTSIDE.

blocks.title: TaskLight microtasks and completion reconciliation
blocks.body: Agents project their queue plans and receipts onto TaskLight cards using post_plan, post_step, post_status, and close_task. When 1552_platform37 ran without microtask mode, reconcile.py returned exit code 1 (MISSING_CLOSE_TASK) because cards were never closed. In 1631_viewpoint_logo, four Gemini agents ran in TaskLight microtask mode (tm1), recording 18 microtasks across 4 tasks: 16 verified, 1 rolled back, and 1 blocked as PARKED:STALE_FRAME, with 0 violations and reconcile rc 0. Across 25 agent events (22 verified), all 3 rewinds—including another director-injected wrong edit—completed with digest_match true and rewindctl audit rc 0.

sections.title: Videos assembled from logs
sections.lede: The takes behind this site's videos are recorded on private displays and logged event by event; operator screen recordings with partial or no logs are marked as such. Because each event carries its time in the video, cuts and captions can be assembled from the log, and models from another family check frames around selected events, so a caption only says what a tool verdict says.

blocks.title: Recording and clock alignment
blocks.body: Every multi-agent take records a private X display at 15 or 30 frames per second using ffmpeg x11grab, written by Claude while Gemini agents operate inside. Wall takes stamp epoch seconds via date immediately after spawning ffmpeg and stamp agent lines on receipt with ts.py, with about 0.5 s of estimated sync error. Multi-agent Blender takes record start_ts_ms in a JSON sidecar alongside the composition log, while an earlier scripted handover take logged wall-clock start time with 1.5 seconds estimated error.

blocks.title: Events, timestamps and receipts
blocks.body: An indexing script compiles clip metadata into MATERIAL_INDEX.json as the source of truth. Each indexed segment binds video window t_in and t_out in seconds, linked to t_video_s, back to a specific line in events.jsonl and its underlying source log. Across the broader pipeline, evidence and proof logs seal artifacts with SHA-256 digests: the strategy asks for each agent stream to be saved with its model, start time and SHA-256, core observations bind frames by sha256 and generation, and demo exports seal frames and events inside digests.json.

blocks.title: An independent frame cross-check
blocks.body: To catch timing drift, reviewers from non-Claude model families—Gemini 4 Carbon Medium and GPT 6.1 Sol—inspected extracted frames at t minus 3, t, and t plus 4 seconds around selected and random events. Among those checks, 25 were visually consistent and 8 were indeterminate when failures produced no screen change or indicators were absent. Because events are timestamped when a tool call returns, visible UI transitions typically appear 1 to 2 seconds before t_video_s, so editors start cuts earlier.

blocks.title: Cuts only from logged verdicts
blocks.body: A four-lane visual review across 45 contact sheets from 19 videos crossed candidate segments with events.jsonl using join_visual.py to populate MONTAJE_SELECCION.json. The editing rule forbids claiming anything absent from logs: segments without events are silent b-roll, and captions quote tool verdicts like NAV_VERIFIED or URL_FRAGMENT_UNOBSERVABLE rather than an agent's self-reported tally. Composite cuts pair the capsule wall with live agent transcripts in side_by_side_3840x1080.mp4 and label time-lapsed stretches explicitly from x2 up to x64.

blocks.title: What never goes into a video
blocks.body: Source warnings exclude dead Blender splash screens, unaccelerated waits, black popup rendering glitches over arXiv, single-capsule crops showing restart bubbles, and frames leaking hostnames or private scratch directories. Provenance rules forbid labeling Claude Sonnet 5.5 handover runs or scripted xdotool clicks as Gemini or live human typing, and forbid presenting deterministic driver guard beats in swarm_take3 as autonomous Gemini behavior. Editors must also reject contradicted agent claims, unlogged polygon counts, and background renders framed as live screen output.

blocks.title: From a recorded demo to a workflow
blocks.body: Separate from full-display video capture, mv_demo.py records manual operator demonstrations on a single capsule with an active identity. It exports sealed events containing text_len without typed characters, a final PNG, any available before/after PNGs, and digests.json, refusing incomplete seals or leaked text fields. An AI then authors a MemoryWeb site and mw.workflow.v1 JSON with locate_wait_ms set to 5000, pinning SHA-256 digests in manifest.json. Validation runs in a disposable copy and never authorizes replay.

sections.title: Robots: AI drives by sight
sections.lede: Outside ViewPoint on a private display, Gemini operated the stock MuJoCo desktop viewer via screenshots and controlled a simulated robot arm from camera images. Across live perturbation takes and a 20-scene benchmark, Gemini matched the exact-pixel oracle (150/150 pointing, 20/20 manipulation), though multi-second latency, exact depth, weld suction, and a benchmark ceiling effect leave real-world limits untested.

blocks.title: MuJoCo as a desktop program (take 2106)
blocks.body: All MuJoCo experiments run outside ViewPoint in simulation on a private display. In take 2106, a Gemini agent operated the stock MuJoCo 4.0.1 desktop viewer purely through screenshots, clicks, and keystrokes via the vision tool, completing 15 passing vision actions over 262 seconds (31 Gemini receipts plus one launcher stop receipt). Gemini enabled contact points and forces, opened control sliders, adjusted the elbow after seeing it touch the top box, knocked down the six-box tower, paused mid-fall, and inspected fixed cameras. Claude wrote the launcher, recorder, and cut scripts.

blocks.title: Gemini as a robot's eye (take 0134)
blocks.body: In take 0134, Gemini served as the visual brain of a simulated robot arm, issuing pixel point, pick, and place commands over 640x480 camera images while programmed inverse kinematics and a weld suction actuator moved the arm. Against MuJoCo ground truth, across six pointing observations (one of them a repeat on the red cube), Gemini named every target correctly, with 1.6 pixels (0.43 centimetres) median error. A test harness shifted the red cube 12.8 centimetres without telling Gemini, causing its first pick to miss by 12.62 centimetres. Re-looking, Gemini re-pointed to 0.21 centimetres error, finishing 2 of 3 picks and 2 of 2 placements at 16.6 seconds median latency.

blocks.title: Camera only, three cubes (take 0146)
blocks.body: Take 0146 restricted Gemini to the robot camera feed until a single final fixed-camera check, removing the HUD hints visible in five full-screen looks during take 0134. Tasked with placing three cubes into the blue box over 390 seconds, Gemini named 11 of 11 points at 3.6 pixels (1.1 centimetres) median error and 9.7 seconds median latency. After the harness shifted the green cube 11.7 centimetres and the orange cube 12.6 centimetres, Gemini observed the displacement visually. All 6 picks succeeded. Each cube's first placement missed, on or behind the box; Gemini saw each miss and corrected it, so 3 of 6 placement attempts succeeded and all 3 cubes ended inside.

blocks.title: A 20-scene benchmark
blocks.body: The 0210 benchmark tested 20 fixed-seed scenes (10 easy, 10 hard with colour distractors, an occluding grey pillar, and plus or minus 30% lighting). Viewing only raw robot renders, Gemini matched the exact-pixel oracle ceiling: 150 of 150 pointing hits (2.5 pixels, 0.69 centimetres median error), 10 of 10 relational queries, and 20 of 20 first-attempt manipulations (83.9% to 100.0% Wilson 95% CI) at 12.31 seconds median latency (16.38 seconds p90). A classic colour detector scored 93 of 150 pointing (50 of 60 easy, 43 of 90 hard) and 10 of 20 manipulations (0 of 10 hard), without language support.

blocks.title: How to read the benchmark
blocks.body: Matching the oracle reveals a ceiling effect: hard scenes challenged a naive colour threshold detector, not Gemini, leaving Gemini's failure boundary unmeasured under dense clutter, strong occlusion, or multi-step commands. The classic detector was intentionally handicapped with thresholds fixed once on five standard colours rather than tuned for maroon, amber, or turquoise. Furthermore, the sample is small at 20 scenes, producing an 83.9% to 100.0% manipulation confidence interval. The tasks are custom rather than LIBERO or public benchmarks, and benchmark episodes start with an empty box instead of the multi-cube collisions seen in take 0146.

blocks.title: Simplifications and limits
blocks.body: All robot runs rely on simulation simplifications: 3D positions come from exact noise-free simulator depth, suction is a weld activated at 1 centimetre, and multi-second thinking pauses freeze the arm, so this is not real-time control. Claude built the launchers, recorders, harness perturbations, independent verification scripts, and benchmark runner, while Gemini wrote the scene, robot server, and benchmark code and ran the episodes. Separately, the vision change detector (vadapt.cu_describe) localized 105 of 105 noiseless synthetic shifts and removals (0.5 to 10 centimetres), but flagged 30 of 30 false changes on idle pairs under simulated sensor noise.
